newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S MANUEL SEES REAL RAND RATE STABILISING.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S MANUEL SEES REAL RAND RATE STABILISING.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Friday that the trade weighted real exchange rate of the rand appeared to have stabilised.
Addressing a conference he also said he expected growth to hold above 2.5 percent next year from 3.0 percent in 1996, with inflation contained in single digits.
The government's macro-economic strategy, announced in June, had contributed to relative market stability, he said.

"Despite the continued ups and downs in the currency following the announcement of the macro-economic strategy, the nominal rate has on average moved in line with the inflation differential between South Africa and our trading partners since the latter part of May," Manuel said.
"The macro-economic strategy deserves some credit in this respect."
Despite a sharp jump in inflation in September, with the annual rate rising to 8.4 percent from 7.5 percent in August, Manuel said he was sanguine about the inflation trend.
"It would appear that inflationary expectations have truly subsided, aided by the more competitive environment that producers in South Africa now have to contend with," he said.
Although the South African economy would inevitably slow next year, the improved outlook for the world economy should cushion the domestic trend, keeping GDP growth above 2.5 percent.
Manuel said the Finance Ministry was busy working on the 1997/98 April-March budget.
"The challenges we face are substantial. I am under no illusion. But let me emphasise the four percent deficit target is not in question," he said.
Some parts of government would face severe belt-tightening, but Manuel said he was convinced there was still too much wasted public expenditure, a hangover from the previous era.
"The coming budget will lead to rationalisation, and in many cases, whole-scale eradication of these expenditures."
However, he said he was determined to protect spending in education, health, welfare, housing and infrastructure.
